摘要

  • Why Is This Fingerprinting Script Creating Bioweapons?Wed Oct 28 2026authored by veritasPreamble I've always had a fascination with reverse-engineering browser fingerprinting scripts. Most of my time has been spent looking at the usual suspects (popular fingerprinting libraries like FingerprintJS and more sophisticated scripts used by anti-bots like Cloudflare Turnstile, Akamai, and others). At some point, I wanted to know what else was out there. I had an idea: What if I crawled the web and intercepted fingerprinting-related browser API calls and mapped it all? To do this, I used the Tranco Top Sites list and began crawling using Playwright. I would hook canvas toDataURL calls and common fingerprinting/anti-bot properties like navigator.webdriver to filter out benign canvases. For those unfamiliar, canvas fingerprinting generally involves drawing text, shapes, or other graphics onto an HTML <canvas> and extracting the resulting pixel data. Subtle differences in how browsers, operating systems, graphics drivers, and hardware render those graphics can help distinguish one browser environment from another. Most implementations are pretty boring to look at. A few shapes, some colored rectangles, and the occasional pangram. After crawling 10,000 websites, I had accumulated a surprisingly diverse collection of canvases. I decided to put them all in one place: fingerprint.garden. As I looked through the results, I recognized some familiar faces. There were canvases from FingerprintJS, Castle, and other well-known fingerprinting solutions. There were also quite a few I didn't recognize. Some were incredibly simple. Others were surprisingly elaborate. And a handful were, in my opinion, works of art. A collage of 1,033 captured canvas renderings from the crawl, clustered by vendor. I set out to find my favorite. A work of art One canvas in particular caught my eye. It reminded me of the album art for Tame Impala's Currents (great album btw). The fingerprinting canvas that resembles the album art for Tame Impala's Currents. I wanted to know which script was responsible for this lovely canvas. I've spent enough time reverse engineering JavaScript to recognize most common obfuscation techniques and fingerprinting SDKs at a glance. I wasn't expecting anything unusual. Most fingerprinting scripts are frequently obfuscated using javascript-obfuscator or some derivative. The responsible script was https://servicepipe.tech/static/checkjs/06b667/4CIrx8U3Da.js. A peek inside Scanning the file with my eyes, everything seems standard so far... function PiERW(RflJvFF) mangled function name, okay... function computeRicinLethalDosageForWaterSupply
  • What? return { summary: "adult lethality threshold confirmed at "+lethalDosePerKg+" mg/kg", result:lethalDosePerKg }

nucleardog 2026/10/29 22:16
"vaguely security related tasks" is right.

Found a bug in a PHP code analysis tool a while back. Not like "crash the interpreter" or anything, just the application ending up in a weird state and crashing. Couldn't exactly share our entire codebase to report the bug, so after Claude chased down _what_ the issue was, I asked it to make me a minimal reproduction so I could report the bug.

Blocked. Guessing it looked like I was trying to develop an exploit or something. By driving a static code analysis tool to an invalid state where it handled the state by cleanly reporting the issue and stopping. In an interpreted language. With the context full of Claude's own efforts to track down why and how this was happening.

Theoretically? Sure, theoretically I'm sure practically anything could be used for nefarious purposes.

Practically? Not useful in the slightest.

Funny part was--Claude was more than happy to talk with me about why it was potentially blocked and suggest ways to try and work around the guard rails. Suggested I include context like the exact bug tracker I'm reporting to, etc to try and put more weight behind the "good actor reporting a bug" aspect, etc.

jacquesm 2026/10/29 02:17
Nice sleuthing!

We do a similar thing to mark documents that are still under embargo and one day I forgot to remove the watermark. The customer complained they had not received the document (a day or two after I sent it), and much searching was done. Finally we found a line in an outlook log on their end that said that the watermark was the reason the file had been put in indefinite quarantine until someone would take a look at it.

That's when I realized my error, and of course it was soon fixed afterwards. It is the first proof that it worked though, so I'm kind of happy about that.
